"Subhuti, what do you think? If a person filled three thousand great thousand-fold worlds <note>a Buddhist cosmological unit representing a billion worlds</note> with the seven treasures <gloss>gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, ruby, and cornelian</gloss> to use for an offering <term>dana</term> <gloss>charity or giving</gloss>, would this person gain much merit <term>punya</term> <gloss>karmic fruitfulness</gloss> through these causes and conditions?"

"Indeed, World-Honored One, this person would gain very much merit through these causes and conditions."

"Subhuti, if merit had a substantial reality, the Thus Come One <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>an epithet of the Buddha</gloss> would not say the merit gained is 'much.' Because merit is empty <note>original: "wu," meaning lacking inherent, permanent substance</note>, the Thus Come One says the merit gained is 'much.'"

<note>Commentary by Huineng:</note> The merit of the seven treasures cannot achieve the fruit of Buddhahood or Awakening <term>Bodhi</term>. Therefore, it is called "empty." Because it is limitless in number and boundary, it is named "much." If one were able to surpass this <note>by attaining formless wisdom</note>, then it would not be called "much."

# Section 20: Detaching from Form and Appearance

<note>Commentary by Huineng:</note> The Three Bodies <term>Trikaya</term> <gloss>the three aspects of the Buddha: the Truth Body, the Reward Body, and the Emanation Body</gloss> are complete. All marks are perfected. Both the self and the Law <term>dharma</term> <gloss>phenomena or teachings</gloss> are forgotten. This state is "non-completion." Therefore, this is followed by the section on detaching from form and appearance.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of merit, explaining that material offerings are considered "much" only because they lack an inherent, permanent substance. It begins Section 20, which questions whether the Buddha can be recognized by his perfected physical form.</summary>
